newsitem.title: USA: Dow powers past 7000 mark amid broad confidence.
newsitem.headline: Dow powers past 7000 mark amid broad confidence.

text.p: The Dow industrials rode a wave of investor confidence to power past the 7,000 milestone on Thursday, capping a breathtaking run that has added 1,000 points to the blue chip index in just four months.

The Dow rose 61 points to close unofficially at 7023. In the past three days, the average has surged 216 points amid broad optimism about the U.S. economy, inflation, corporate profits and interest rates.
Early in the session, the Dow staged a series of brief forays above 7000 but failed to mount a serious charge until the recently dormant bond market sprang to life.

"This market is interpreting everything positively right now," said Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears Benzak Salomon and Farrell. "Today, all of a sudden the bond market got its legs and pretty soon, stocks were dancing."
The bond rally, which began just after the U.S. Treasury sold $10.0 billion in bonds in a quarterly auction, drove the rate on the benchmark 30-year bond down to 6.63 percent.
Stoking the demand for stocks is a strong U.S. dollar, analysts said, citing a variety of reasons the currency's recent rise has lifted share prices.

"The dollar's strength is diminshing fears of inflation because a strong dollar tends to lower the cost of imports," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "Clearly, inflation has always been a critical variable for the market."
Another byproduct is renewed international demand for U.S. financial assets.

While the favorable economic backdrop remained intact, stocks still needed evidence of continued corporate earnings growth to sustain their rally. The just-concluded wave of fourth-quarter results provided that, analysts said.

"There are two things that matter -- interest rates and corporate earnings," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "Rates are coming down and corporate earnings are still showing powerful growth."
Even with all the elements of a positive market environment in place, several analysts warned that the bull market seemed to be developing a cult of personality.

"People are starting to treat these top 50 stocks as collectors' items," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "We need to enjoy this but not necessarily take on more risk at these levels."
The market rally also pulled broader indices to all-time highs. The S&P 500 index rose 9.05 points to a record 811.82, and the NYSE Composite rose 4.54 points to a record 424.42.
The Nasdaq Composite gained 11.85 points to close at 1370.81, still about 18 points shy of its record 1388.06, set on January 22.
Merrill Lynch and Co Inc led financial stocks higher. The shares, which were added to the Goldman Sachs recommended list, jumped 8-1/2 to 96-1/2.
Citicorp rose four to 123-1/2, and BankAmerica Corp gained 5-1/8 to 123.

Pharmaceutical shares were also strong. Merck and Co rose 3-3/4 to 99-5/8, and Pfizer Inc rose 2-3/8 to 96. Johnson & Johnson gained 1-1/8 to 61-3/4 after A.G. Edwards raised its rating on the shares to buy.

There were losers among the crowd. Galileo Corp plummeted 11-3/4 to 6-7/8 after warning it expected to post a loss in fiscal 1997. The company cited the loss of a key contract with Xerox Corp that accounted for nearly half its revenues last year. Xerox shares fell 3/8 to 56-1/8.
Donnelley Entertainment Solutions Inc slid 11-3/4 to 12 after announcing its fiscal 1996 results would fall well short of Wall Street estimates.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
